newsitem.title: USA: Traders divided over LME aluminum backwardation.
newsitem.headline: Traders divided over LME aluminum backwardation.

text.p: Aluminum traders are divided over whether the aluminum price, currently at its highest level in nearly five months, is fundamentally justified or being distorted by speculative squeezes.
The benchmark cash-to-three-month spread is trading in backwardation, which would appear to indicate physical tightness.
And, indeed, London Metal Exchange warehouse stockpiles have fallen at a rate of 11,628 tonnes a week since Jan 16. But some traders believe something more sinister is at hand.
The cash-to-three-month contango was $3/$5 at 0900 EDT/1300 GMT against $28 two weeks ago. The LME three-month price soared to $1,689.50/$1,690.50 from Friday's evening evaluation price of $1,685.

"With the spreads coming in, many traders will be tempted to ask 'Is this for real,'" said Christopher Langguth, senior vice president of Mitsui & Co's New York trading desk. "We have every reason to believe it's for real."

He added, "It comes as something as a surprise in the middle of the summer when demand is usually slower. But there's been significant fund interest. Stocks have been dwindling at a significant rate of withdrawal. This market seems poised for higher numbers."
The alternative theory is that one or several players are buying up significant long positions in August, and squeezing speculators that are short the August prompt date, which is Aug 20.
At the center of this speculation is Barclays Metals, which has been accused of being on both sides of the market.

"They're buying everything in sight nearby," said one northeastern merchant. "At the same time they're forward selling into 1998. The producers are also joining in the forward selling and the result is a healthy little backwardation."

"It's absolutely a manipulation," another trader said. "Show me a reason why the cash-to-threes would narrow from a $28 contango to a $100 backwardation in one week. It's a game and it shows that you can no longer trust the terminal market."
But on July 17, Alcoa chairman Paul O'Neill quoted rumors that Barclays was trying to keep prices lower.

"They did not like the direction the metal price was taking and so they dumped the 10,000 tonnes onto warrants in an attempt to influence the price going down," he said at the time, refering to the first significant increase in LME stockpiles in six months.
Interestingly, some traders have accused O'Neill's remarks of having the opposite effect on the market. "Alcoa is no better than Barclays," said one trader. "Remarks like that get the market juiced."
Neither Alcoa nor Barclays immediately returned phone calls requesting comment.

O'Neill's remarks touch on a contentious issue in the aluminum market. Some sources suggest that the LME stock decline isn't the result of consumption but more the result of "white-lining," the removal of metal from LME warrant but not actually moved from the LME warehouse. Starting Oct 1, LME will begin reporting such practices.
LME chief executive David King didn't return phone calls requesting comment on the suggestion that the aluminum market is being manipulated.
"Manipulation is a very strong word," said Malcolm Freeman, a trader with GNI Ltd. "I don't believe that this squeeze is deliberate or being engineered by anyone in particular."
The LME zinc market is also attracting attention for its steep backwardation and rumors of distortion.

Physical demand for aluminum has been steady, dealers said, with Midwest premiums at 4.50-5.00 cents over LME cash. Some dealers, however, say the backwardation has softened physical premiums because there's no incentive to carry metal.
"Demand has been fine. No one is complaining," the trader continued. "But in the middle of the mummer it makes absolutely no sense for prices to rally $100 in one week."
(New York Commodity Desk, 212-859-1646)
